newsitem.title: USA: Brokers DLJ, PaineWebber post strong profits.
newsitem.headline: Brokers DLJ, PaineWebber post strong profits.

text.p: Brokerage companies Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette Inc. and PaineWebber Group Inc. reported strong fourth quarter earnings Monday, aided by the booming stock market as well as their mergers and underwriting businesses.
Alex. Brown Inc. also reported stronger profits.

Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette said its net income for the quarter rose to $73.1 million, or $1.15 a share, from $57.6 million, or 93 cents a share a year ago. The results blew past Wall Street's expectations of 96 cents a share.
New York-based DLJ said its revenues for the quarter rose to $952.6 million from $797.4 million.
"It was a very strong quarter across the board" for DLJ said Brown Brothers Harriman analyst Raphael Soifer.
During the quarter, DLJ benefitted from sharply higher fee revenues, a function of the firm's efforts to build its merger business, its Chairman John Chalsty said in an interview.
"Fees were very strong and we were quite pleased about that because they reflect great growth in our merger and acquisitions practice," he said.
Chalsty said he was optimistic about the firm's 1997 prospects, citing mergers and underwriting as strong points.
"We're not in fear and trembling of 1997," he said. "We're going into this year with a fair amount of optimism. We have a significant backlog and more importantly significant momentum."

For the full year DLJ said its net income climbed to a record $291.3 million, or $4.55 a share, from $179.1 million, or $3.08 a share. Revenues for the year expanded to $3.5 billion from $2.8 billion.
DLJ's stock ended up 37.5 cents at $37 on the New York Stock Exchange.

PaineWebber Group, also based in New York, said its net income for the fourth quarter grew by 56 percent to $91.5 million, or 91 cents a share, from $58.8 million, or 52 cents a share. Its profits also topped Wall Street forecasts.

"We are pleased with the consistency and improvement our 1996 results represent, and we believe they reflect a great deal more than the firm's ability to prosper in a vigorous bull market," said Donald Marron, PaineWebber's chairman.
Revenues for the quarter rose to $1.47 billion from $1.37 billion, while annual revenues rose to $5.71 billion from $5.32 billion.

Net income for the full year soared to a record $364.4 million, or $3.59 a share, from $80.8 million, or 54 cents a share. The year-earlier period included a charge related to limited partnership investment issues.
PaineWebber's shares ended off 12.5 cents at $31.25 on the NYSE.

Baltimore, Md.-based Alex. Brown Inc. reported fourth quarter net income of $37.3 million, or $1.51 a share, compared with $33.2 million and $1.39 a share in 1995's fourth quarter. For the full year it reported net income of $154.1 million, or $6.28 a share, up from $95.6 million, or $4.11 a share.
Revenues for the quarter rose to $264.4 million from $246.7 million. Annual revenues climbed to $1.1 billion from $809.4 million.
The results for the year were the highest in the company's 196-year history, the firm said.
Alex. Brown said its investment banking revenues surged 41 percent to $414.9 million, due primarily to a robust public offering underwriting market.
Alex. Brown's shares ended up $2 at $49.875 on the NYSE.
